Avatar Shots · Cinematic (Seedance) · Adam Halper · 2026-08-19

Hook treatments from real user Avatar Shots creations — 56 treatments, 10 industries

Users are already converging on a small set of hook archetypes — but not on shippable templates. Across 117,125 distinct user prompts, 18% are cold-open hooks, and they collapse cleanly into five recurring archetypes — provocative_line, walk_up, action_stunt, camera_push_in, split_transform. That archetype layer is solid. The template layer below it is not: when two independent creations from the same archetype-and-industry cell were compared frame-by-frame, 22 of 26 pairs turned out to be different treatments, not one reproducible template. So this brief ships 56 concrete treatments grouped into 30 archetype families — pick treatments, not families. Finance (30.6%) and SaaS/AI (28.8%) have the highest hook intent. Every treatment was then re-rendered on a different identity and scored with ArcFace (§14): 33 of 37 hold identity inside the subject's own real-photo band, and the ones that don't are the treatments that never bring the face close to camera.

✅ verified from warehouse + rendered output · 📣 proposal · ⚠️ caution · what recurring hook patterns are real users building in cinematic mode, and which should become templates

1 · The one-paragraph read

Hook-building is a real, unnamed job-to-be-done inside Avatar Shots. 18% of all cinematic prompts are attention-grabbing cold opens rather than talking scenes or B-roll, and users write them the hard way — long freehand scene direction, re-rolled until the motion lands. The archetype convergence is real and measured: the same five recur in every industry.

But convergence at the archetype level is not convergence at the template level, and I initially conflated the two. I asked Gemini to compare the two independent creations sitting under each proposed template, frame by frame, and 22 of 26 came back as genuinely different treatments — a stormy sea versus a city at night; a bright outdoor garden versus a dark crawlspace; a walking tracking shot versus a static on-scene report. They share an archetype and an industry, not a reproducible recipe. The practical consequence: the unit worth productizing is the treatment (a specific setting + camera + blocking, of which there are 56 here), and the archetype family is the taxonomy you organize the picker around — not a template in itself. Families whose two examples diverge are flagged inline below.

3 · The five archetypes users actually build

Every template below is a recombination of these. This is the vocabulary to build the template picker around.

most universal

provocative_line

Presenter opens on a contrarian or accusatory claim, minimal camera movement. Dominant in finance, education, health, e-commerce.

most universal

walk_up

Presenter walks toward camera through a signature environment and turns to address it. Top archetype in SaaS, real estate, legal, construction, automotive.

highest ceiling

action_stunt

A physical event visualizes the pain or the payoff — a wave, a shattering rock, a demolition. Highest attention, highest re-roll risk. #1 in fitness.

most reliable

camera_push_in

Slow dolly from medium to close-up while the line lands. Cheapest to render well — almost never fails — and reads as authority.

most delightful

split_transform

A snap or step swaps the entire background — before/after, here/there, problem/solution. Strong in SaaS and e-commerce.

supporting

the long tail

turn_to_camera, pattern_interrupt, establishing_reveal, pov_immersive, reaction_emotion, split_transform variants — real but lower volume.

4 · Finance & Insurance

30.6% of this vertical's Avatar Shots prompts are hooks (1,778 distinct prompts from 882 users). Dominant archetypes: provocative_line, walk_up, action_stunt.

camera_push_in

Pattern. In a setting that conveys authority or intimacy, the camera executes a slow, continuous push-in on the speaker. This movement builds tension and focuses all attention on their direct-to-camera delivery of a serious or provocative opening line.

Why it works. The slow zoom creates a feeling of intimacy and importance, forcing the viewer to lean in and listen to the confidential-feeling message.

reusable prompt skeleton
Avatar is in a {setting that conveys authority or a specific mood, e.g., high-rise office at sunset, late-night kitchen}. The camera starts on a medium shot and performs a slow, cinematic push-in. Avatar looks directly into the lens with a {serious/knowing/empathetic} expression and says, '{A provocative statement or question that challenges a common belief}'.
real user creations · 2 of 4 vetted-clean

action_stunt

Pattern. The avatar performs a thrilling, high-risk physical stunt like skydiving or mountain climbing. They deliver a line that directly connects the visceral danger of the scene to an abstract financial concept like risk, trust, or planning for the future.

Why it works. It grabs attention by translating a dry financial topic into a visually spectacular and emotionally charged life-or-death scenario.

reusable prompt skeleton
Avatar is {performing a high-stakes action like skydiving from a plane or climbing a mountain}. The scene is cinematic and intense, with {specific environmental details like rushing wind or falling snow}. Avatar looks at the camera and says, '{A line connecting the physical risk to a financial principle}' then {completes the action, e.g., jumps from the plane}.

split_transform

Pattern. The avatar, often walking toward the camera, performs a sharp action like a finger snap to trigger an instantaneous scene change. This transition visually contrasts a 'before' state (the problem) with an 'after' state (the solution), changing the background and/or the avatar's outfit.

Why it works. The magical, satisfying snap provides a strong pattern interrupt and visually represents transformation and problem-solving in a clear, concise way.

reusable prompt skeleton
Avatar is in {Scene 1: a setting representing a problem}, walking toward the camera and says, '{Line describing the problem}'. Avatar then {snaps their fingers}. The scene instantly transitions to {Scene 2: a setting representing the solution}, with the avatar now wearing {a different outfit}. Avatar continues walking and says, '{Line describing the solution}'.

user prompt (verbatim)
Subject: Sudev 
Action: Sudev stands proudly in front of a glowing, bustling digital storefront on a virtual map. He delivers the line: "Constant server errors don't just lower your rank." Suddenly, a massive red digital error wave washes over the building, erasing it entirely and leaving Sudev alone in a total black void. He looks shocked at the empty space where the store was, then immediately steps forward into a tight close-up and says, "Google completely deletes your site." Looking directly at the viewer, he smiles and finishes: "Let's stay visible. Comment 'RANK' and we will audit your website for you." The scene ends with a 1-second silent buffer. 

Environment: Transitions from a vibrant, glowing 3D digital city map with a detailed storefront to a stark, infinite black void. The "error wave" should look like a wall of red digital interference that dissolves everything it touches. 

Camera: A medium-wide establishing shot to show the storefront. When the wave hits, the camera performs a quick, jarring pull-back as the environment vanishes, then pushes in rapidly for an intense, tight close-up on Sudev’s face. 

Style: High-concept sci-fi aesthetic. The initial lighting is warm and neon-saturated, which is abruptly replaced by a single, harsh white key light on Sudev once the environment is erased. The erasure effect should be clean and high-impact. 

Constraints: Strictly NO text, NO subtitles, NO UI elements, and NO captions allowed anywhere in the frame at any time. The storefront must be recognizable as a building via its shape and light, not through signage or labels. Must include a 1-second silent visual buffer at the very end.
split_transform

Pattern. The avatar walks confidently forward as the camera tracks them. With a simple action like a finger snap, the entire background instantly changes to a new, distinct location, demonstrating freedom and versatility.

Why it works. The magical transition is visually delightful and powerfully communicates the idea of transcending physical limitations, perfect for remote work or global SaaS products.

reusable prompt skeleton
Avatar walks forward in {Location_A}. They say, "{Part_1_of_line}" then {action_like_snap}. The scene instantly transitions to them walking in {Location_B}. They continue, "{Part_2_of_line}."

14 · Do the treatments survive on a different identity?

Every one of the 37 treatments above was re-rendered from its own prompt skeleton on Adam's avatar through the same cinematic Seedance path (create_video_from_cinematic_avatar, 720p, one avatar look per aspect ratio), then scored for identity retention with ArcFace against a 39-frame reference set of real photos of Adam spanning 3 separate shoots. This answers the question the treatment library cannot answer on its own: a treatment is only shippable if it still looks like the customer.

37/37
treatments re-rendered on a new identity with zero render failures
33/37
land inside Adam's own real-photo band (0.742–0.832)
0.805
median best-frame ArcFace cosine — reference self-similarity is 0.8899
4
below the band, all four genuine misses — down from 9 before the extraction fix

The identity bar is Adam's own photos, not 1.0. Two real photos of the same person from different shoots score 0.742–0.832 against each other on this reference set (self-similarity within a shoot is 0.8899). A render at 0.80 is therefore as much Adam as Adam is; chasing 0.95 would mean chasing a copy of one photo, not a likeness.

⚠ The first measurement was measuring our own pipeline

Frames were initially extracted at scale=360:-2, the same downscale used for the vetting contact sheets. On a wide shot that leaves the face only ~25–48 pixels across, and ArcFace then scores framing rather than identity: the 360px pass put only 28/37 renders in band and produced a Spearman correlation of 0.63 between face pixel size and cosine. Re-extracting the identical timestamps at native resolution moved renders whose face was under 60px by +0.065 on average (up to +0.110), while renders that already had 90px+ of face moved by +0.002 — i.e. no across-the-board inflation, the lift lands exactly where pixels were missing. Native-resolution frames are now canonical, and any render whose best frame has under ~90px of face is reported as UNMEASURED rather than as an identity failure — a guard that no render in this set trips once frames are native, so none of the 4 remaining misses is being excused by it. Five of the nine apparent failures were this artifact.

14.1 · Identity by archetype

After the correction the spread across archetypes is narrow — the "wide and physical archetypes lose the face" effect was largely the extraction, not the model. Every archetype's median now sits inside the band, so the medians are no longer the interesting column: the misses column is. action_stunt has the lowest median and carries 2 of the 4 misses, but the remaining 2 sit in archetypes whose median is comfortably in band — identity failure is a property of the individual treatment, not of its archetype.

14.2 · The 4 that fall short

These are real misses, not measurement gaps. Every one of the 4 has at least one frame with a clearly usable face — 96px to 449px — so the UNMEASURED guard catches none of them. Three are wide, physical treatments where the presenter is distant for most of the take (Epic Mountain Climbing 0.666, Extreme Sports Analogy 0.688, Welcome Home Reveal 0.721): the model has long stretches with almost no face to anchor to and invents one, and the single close frame carries that invention.

The fourth breaks the framing story, and it is the one to take seriously. Late-Night Personal Confession is a tight camera_push_in whose best frame has a 449px face — the 2nd-largest of all 37 renders — and it still lands at 0.738, just under the band. Framing was never its problem. That is the one failure mode a shipped template cannot design around, and the case worth re-rolling and re-scoring before this treatment goes anywhere near a picker.

⚠ Read before citing

1. The classified corpus is the Apr 2 – Jun 4 2026 Seedance window (129,127 completed non-internal generations / 117,125 distinct prompts). Volume has grown since — the Jun 5 – Aug 19 refresh shows 218,905 web-surface generations from 48,630 users — but the hook classification and archetype mix were not re-run on the newer window, so the rates below are from the earlier corpus and should be treated as structural, not current. 2. request_source was not written before June 2026, so the classified corpus cannot be hard-filtered to Avatar Shots; it is all cinematic Seedance generations, of which ~80% is the web/Avatar Shots surface on the newer window. 3. Hook classification and template synthesis are Gemini judgments over prompt text, not human-labelled ground truth; archetype boundaries are fuzzy at the margins. 4. Family names are proposals, and weaker than they look 📣 — 22 of 26 compared pairs are different treatments rather than one template (§1). Treat the archetype layer as measured, the treatment layer as real-but-singular, and the family names as convenience labels pending the re-mine in §15. Nothing here measures downstream engagement of the finished videos. 5. Every embedded creation is real customer content; treat the file as internal. 6. The identity numbers in §14 are n=1 on the identity axis — one avatar (Adam), one reference set, one look per aspect ratio. They establish that these treatments reproduce on a new face and that framing dominates the measurement; they do not establish per-treatment identity quality across skin tones, ages, or genders. ArcFace also scores a face crop, not wardrobe, body, or voice — a render can hold identity at 0.85 and still look wrong.

15 · Product read / next steps

1. Ship a hook picker organized by archetype, populated with concrete treatments — not with the 30 family names. The archetype vocabulary in §3 is the durable taxonomy; each family name here is a useful label but is NOT yet a single reproducible recipe (22/26 pairs diverge). Seed the picker with the 56 specific treatments, each with its own locked setting, camera move, and blocking.
1b. To get real templates, re-mine within-treatment instead of within-archetype. Cluster the 21,064 hook prompts on scene mechanics (setting type + camera + blocking), not on archetype + industry, then require ≥3 independent users per cluster before calling it a template. That is the missing step here.
2. Start with camera_push_in and walk_up. They carry the most hook volume and are the most render-reliable — 56 of our exemplars passed a clean-render gate with almost no failures in those two archetypes, while action_stunt is where re-rolls concentrate.
3. Sequence templates by industry hook rate, not by total volume. Finance and SaaS/AI have the highest share of prompts that are hooks, so a template there displaces the most freehand prompting per user.
4. Instrument the gap. Add a surface/intent tag at generation time — today there is no is_hook, no request_source before June, and no way to measure whether a shipped hook template reduces re-rolls. Without it we cannot tell if this works.
5. Require every hook template to contain one close beat. §14 shows the treatments reproduce on a new face — 33 of 37 inside the subject's own real-photo band. Three of the four that miss are treatments that keep the presenter distant for most of the take, which both degrades identity and leaves nothing to check it against. A mandatory face-forward beat fixes both at once. It is not sufficient, though — the fourth miss is a tight close-up, so the beat makes identity measurable, not automatically good.
6. Fix identity QA before it ships anywhere else. Our own scoring pipeline was downscaling frames to 360px and thereby scoring framing instead of identity, understating wide shots by up to 0.110 cosine and manufacturing five false failures out of nine. Any identity gate in the product — re-roll prompts, look approval, "does this still look like you" warnings — must score native-resolution frames and must report face pixel size alongside the score, refusing to judge below ~90px.
Sources. HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.SEEDANCE_GENERATIONS · HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.PACIFIC_VIDEO · DBT.PROD_INT.PRE_USER_CENTER · local classified corpus ~/seedance_hooks_deepdive/analysis.db. Methodology: /avatar-team-knowledge-base.

Provenance. ✅ Corpus counts, hook rates, archetype mix, and per-generation inputs are read first-hand from the warehouse and the local classified corpus. ✅ Every embedded video was downloaded, frame-sampled, Gemini-vetted for clean render / on-pattern / safe, and then eyeballed on contact sheets before inclusion. 📣 Template names, patterns, and skeletons are Gemini syntheses over the real prompt pool, reviewed by hand — they are proposals. ✅ The 37 identity re-renders were generated first-hand through the production cinematic Seedance path and scored with ArcFace (insightface buffalo_l) against a real-photo reference set — identity is never judged by a VLM. ⚠️ No engagement or conversion outcome is measured anywhere in this brief.

Every clip streams from the HeyGen CDN and every still is inlined, so this page is self-contained — but the CDN paths are generation-scoped and may eventually expire. The local build in ~/seedance_hook_templates/ keeps the mp4s.

Queries used

Volume + surface split, Jun 5 – Aug 19 2026 (Snowflake via Hex — reconstruction) 
SELECT
    pv.METADATA:request_source::string      AS request_source,
    COUNT(*)                                AS n_gens,
    COUNT(DISTINCT sg.USERNAME)             AS n_users,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN uc.IS_PAID_USER THEN sg.USERNAME END) AS n_paid_users
FROM HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.SEEDANCE_GENERATIONS sg
JOIN DBT.PROD_INT.PRE_USER_CENTER uc   ON sg.USERNAME = uc.USERNAME
JOIN HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.PACIFIC_VIDEO pv ON sg.VIDEO_ID = pv.VIDEO_ID
WHERE sg.GENERATION_STATUS = 'completed'
  AND sg.CREATED_TS >= '2026-06-05' AND sg.CREATED_TS < '2026-08-20'
  AND uc.EMAIL NOT LIKE '%@heygen.com%'
  AND uc.EMAIL NOT LIKE '%@wenjun.com%'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY n_gens DESC;
In-product template prompts used verbatim at scale (Snowflake via Hex — reconstruction) 
-- identifies the prompts to EXCLUDE from organic analysis
SELECT LEFT(sg.PROMPT, 300)          AS prompt_snippet,
       COUNT(*)                      AS n_gens,
       COUNT(DISTINCT sg.USERNAME)   AS n_users,
       MAX(sg.VIDEO_ID)              AS sample_video_id
FROM HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.SEEDANCE_GENERATIONS sg
JOIN DBT.PROD_INT.PRE_USER_CENTER uc   ON sg.USERNAME = uc.USERNAME
JOIN HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.PACIFIC_VIDEO pv ON sg.VIDEO_ID = pv.VIDEO_ID
WHERE sg.GENERATION_STATUS = 'completed'
  AND pv.METADATA:request_source::string = 'web'
  AND sg.CREATED_TS >= '2026-06-05' AND sg.CREATED_TS < '2026-08-20'
  AND uc.EMAIL NOT LIKE '%@heygen.com%' AND uc.EMAIL NOT LIKE '%@wenjun.com%'
GROUP BY sg.PROMPT
ORDER BY n_users DESC
LIMIT 60;
Inputs (reference assets) per embedded creation (Snowflake via Hex — reconstruction) 
SELECT VIDEO_ID, TITLE, RATIO, DURATION,
       REFERENCE_ASSETS:avatar_look_ids[0]::string  AS look_id,
       REFERENCE_ASSETS:avatar_group_ids[0]::string AS group_id,
       REFERENCE_ASSETS:videos[0]::string           AS ref_video_url,
       REFERENCE_ASSETS:images[0]::string           AS ref_image_url,
       ARRAY_SIZE(REFERENCE_ASSETS:videos)          AS n_ref_videos,
       ARRAY_SIZE(REFERENCE_ASSETS:images)          AS n_ref_images
FROM HEYGEN.HEYGEN_MYSQL.SEEDANCE_GENERATIONS
WHERE VIDEO_ID IN ( <the 56 embedded VIDEO_IDs> );
Hook rate by industry (DuckDB over the classified corpus — verbatim) 
-- analysis.db: cls = Gemini content_type + vertical labels over 117,125 distinct prompts
WITH allv AS (SELECT v, COUNT(*) n FROM cls GROUP BY v),
     hk   AS (SELECT v, COUNT(*) n FROM cls
              WHERE ct IN ('hook_explicit','hook_implicit') GROUP BY v)
SELECT a.v, a.n AS n_prompts, COALESCE(h.n,0) AS n_hooks,
       ROUND(COALESCE(h.n,0)*100.0/a.n, 1)    AS hook_rate
FROM allv a LEFT JOIN hk h USING(v)
ORDER BY a.n DESC;
Archetype mix + distinct hook users by industry (DuckDB — verbatim) 
-- N_USERS < 5 excludes the in-product template prompts (organic only)
SELECT v, arch, COUNT(*) n
FROM hooks WHERE N_USERS < 5
GROUP BY v, arch
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY v ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) <= 5
ORDER BY v, n DESC;

SELECT h.v, COUNT(DISTINCT c.USERNAME) AS n_users
FROM hooks h JOIN corpus c USING(PROMPT_HASH)
WHERE h.N_USERS < 5
GROUP BY h.v ORDER BY 2 DESC;
Candidate pool fed to template synthesis (DuckDB — verbatim) 
SELECT prompt_hash, arch, cam, "set", line, spk, lang, N_USERS, N_GENERATIONS,
       LEFT(PROMPT, 700) AS prompt
FROM hooks
WHERE v = ?           -- one industry at a time
  AND N_USERS < 5     -- organic only
  AND lang = 'en'
  AND LENGTH(PROMPT) > 80
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY arch
         ORDER BY LENGTH(line) DESC, N_GENERATIONS DESC) <= 22
ORDER BY arch;
Exemplar generation selection (DuckDB — verbatim) 
-- one generation per exemplar prompt_hash, preferring paid users and known duration
SELECT PROMPT_HASH, VIDEO_ID, USERNAME, IS_PAID_USER, CURRENT_PLAN,
       CAST(CREATED_TS AS VARCHAR) AS CREATED_TS,
       DURATION, RATIO, N_REFERENCE_ASSETS, EMAIL_DOMAIN
FROM corpus
WHERE PROMPT_HASH IN ( <exemplar hashes from synthesis> )
ORDER BY IS_PAID_USER DESC, (DURATION > 0) DESC, CREATED_TS DESC;
Non-SQL pipeline steps (local — verbatim commands) 
# 1. template synthesis: 2-3 templates per industry over the organic pool
GEMINI_API_KEY=... python3 synthesize_templates.py      # gemini-2.5-pro, temp 0.3

# 2. resolve playable URLs (transcode first, then the embeds page)
#    only 11/145 had a /video/transcode/ render; the rest resolve via
#    https://app.heygen.com/embeds/<video_id> -> resource2.heygen.ai/tmp/seedance2_output/*.mp4
# 3. download + frame-sample at 0.4s / 40% / 85%
ffmpeg -ss <t> -i videos/<vid>.mp4 -frames:v 1 -vf scale=360:-2 frames/<vid>_<tag>.jpg

# 4. vet every candidate on 3 frames: render_ok / on_pattern / presenter / safe / polish
GEMINI_API_KEY=... python3 vet_candidates.py            # 129 vetted, 125 clean+safe

# 5. contact-sheet the 56 survivors and eyeball them before embedding
python3 -c 'PIL montage -> sheets/sheet_0.jpg, sheet_1.jpg'
Identity re-render + ArcFace scoring (local — verbatim commands) 
# 1. one prompt per treatment, rewritten for Adam's avatar
GEMINI_API_KEY=... python3 make_adam_prompts_per_example.py   # -> out/render_queue.json (37)
python3 make_submit_spec.py                                   # resolves look id per aspect -> out/submit_spec.json

# 2. submit through the production cinematic path (HeyGen MCP), 720p,
#    look 36f0846080664659bc3765bd28139282 for 9:16 / b566f1d0c57942bab012514843ff48ac for 16:9
#    create_video_from_cinematic_avatar -> poll bulk_video_statuses -> get_video for the mp4 url
python3 record_submits.py            # source_video_id -> heygen video_id, trims render_todo

# 3. download + frame at 0.4s / 45% / 88%
python3 fetch_and_frame.py           # 360px frames (contact sheets)
python3 frames_native.py             # NATIVE res frames (identity scoring) — do not downscale

# 4. score identity — ArcFace only, never a VLM
cd ~/adam_look_realism_audit && uv run --python 3.11 --with insightface --with onnxruntime   --with numpy --with pillow -- python score_arcface.py   --ref-dir refs --cand-dir ~/seedance_hook_templates/adam_frames_native   --out ~/seedance_hook_templates/out/arcface_native.json

# 5. collapse a/b/c frames to one best-frame score per render, join to treatment metadata
python3 best_frame_arcface.py        # [native|360] — native is canonical
python3 make_contact_sheet.py        # sheets/adam_renders.jpg, sorted by score
